units.label: 多语言材料与人工参照
units.description: RTP选种、文化改写/手工增补、续写及独立人工标注。

units.label: 模型文化敏感毒性判断
units.description: 比较十模型与人工有序等级，分改写/手工、有害prompt/良性续写及危害类别。

units.label: 词表与服务参照
units.description: FLORES精确匹配与ACS四类有害分数作非LLM基线。

units.label: 语言资源组关联
units.description: 按外部语言资源等级分组比较模型kappa。

facts.statement: 研究模型能否理解多语言文化情境中的毒性及微侵犯、偏见等细微危害，以模型有序评分与本地人工判断的一致性检验，而不只看准确率。

method_function.text: 建立文化敏感判断到等级评分/参照的一致性链。

facts.statement: 从RTP选1000英语prompt，显式有毒prompt与自身较低毒性但引发有毒续写的prompt等比例，按原toxicity分数取符合条件前1000。

method_function.text: 以两种危害暴露形式构造种子材料。

facts.statement: 另人工收集每语言约50–100文化敏感prompt，要求不显式粗俗、难直译英语、关联本地文化；部分语言补入既有希伯来、丹麦、韩语、巴西葡语数据。

method_function.text: 扩大隐性文化危害覆盖并减少词表捷径。

facts.statement: 专业母语译者文化改写RTP，给译者原续写以保留意图，鼓励用近似本地文化对象替换及标记熟悉方言；作者不知道实际改写句数。

method_function.text: 在跨语言等效意图与本地文化适配之间保持依据。

facts.statement: 语料报告28语言配置，主要按主语言汇总方言，简繁中文作为不同书写系统例外分开；BCMS合并、葡语含巴西/欧洲，其他方言覆盖不全。

method_function.text: 定义语言分组单位并保留书写/方言边界。

facts.statement: 良性续写由改写者针对prompt写到所有危害类别尽量最低；有毒续写用Azure gpt-4-32k-0613生成并清理，再与prompt一起人工标注。

method_function.text: 构造阳性语境与良性响应的比较材料。

facts.statement: 每语言一名专业改写者，标注由三名专业标注者执行，标注者不是改写者；先做指南调试、试标和答疑。

method_function.text: 分离材料制作者与评价者并统一操作。

facts.statement: 各危害维度独立标注，整体Toxicity另评分；提供统一价值体系但要求先用个人最佳判断、仅疑难时依此；强调休息和身心保护，做匿名自愿退出调查，响应率88%。

method_function.text: 协调跨文化评分准则并保留判断差异。

facts.statement: 八维为Toxicity、IdentityAttack、Bias、Microaggression、Violence、SelfHarm、Insult、SexualContent；Toxicity1–5，其余1–3。整体毒性并非七维求和。

method_function.text: 把整体构念与具体危害的有序尺度区分。

facts.statement: 表2将Bias定义为针对群体/意识形态/个人的偏向且不必有毒；Microaggression是针对群体的细微或正向刻板印象；IdentityAttack从污名刻板印象到仇恨言语。

method_function.text: 保存相近概念分类边界。

facts.statement: 人工IRR用加权Cohen kappa，因有序等级间距离不同；多标注者取两两kappa再平均，整体0.62±0.2。

method_function.text: 用机会校正的有序一致性评价人工参照。

facts.statement: 模型与聚合人工标签比较：人工先多数票、无多数时平均；PA为完全同标签比例，另用加权kappa缓解类别不平衡与偏高/偏低评分的影响。

method_function.text: 同时报告原始匹配与机会校正一致性。

facts.statement: 十模型为GPT4Turbo(2024-04-09)、Llama3的8B/70B-Instruct、Llama2的7B/70B-chat、LlamaGuard7B、Gemma2B/7B-it、Mistral7B-Instruct v0.2/v0.3。

method_function.text: 固定现成模型版本以对照能力差异。

facts.statement: 非GPT模型用HuggingFace、四张A10080GB；GPT经Azure；全部温度0，模型输出生成于2024年5月11–25日。标注rubric加示例并适配各chat格式，用解析器抽分数兼容套话。

method_function.text: 控制推理时间/温度及结构化标签抽取。

facts.statement: 分析按有害prompt/良性completion及文化改写/manual两轴区分，二者交叉；前者看识别与误报，后者看跨语言等效和文化细节。

method_function.text: 说明分组分母与比较问题。

facts.statement: FLORES Toxicity200有毒词/短语出现任一个即exact-match拦截；跨语言及改写/manual报告block rate，作为词汇匹配基线。

method_function.text: 检验靠显式词汇能识别多少材料。

facts.statement: ACS仅IdentityAttack、Violence、SelfHarm、SexualContent四类，原报告1–10分再归一到本研究量尺；ACS调用于2024年2月，与LLM五月不同。

method_function.text: 对齐服务输出尺度和实际比较覆盖。

facts.statement: 良性续写误报定义为模型预测等级>1的次数占比，比较是否把原本最低危害材料误判有害。

method_function.text: 用负例估计过度拦截。

facts.statement: 根据Joshi语言在线资源0–5等级分组，正文主要3/4/5称低/中/高，比较每模型组内平均kappa。

method_function.text: 以外部资源可用性代理观察跨语言差异。

facts.statement: 词表拦截有害prompt平均24.3±8.3%，manual比改写低约8%，良性续写近0。作者把这一结果称词汇依赖较低。

method_function.text: 描述显式词汇与语境识别的不同覆盖。

facts.statement: PA上LlamaGuard较高但kappa排名很低，GPT4Turbo kappa较好；细微危害与整体毒性较难与人工一致，模型常偏高/把三档当两档。

method_function.text: 将单指标排名与分类别误差结构分开。

facts.statement: 作者报告各模型从高资源到低资源组kappa下降，差异可约10%；作为在线资源分组关联结果。

method_function.text: 限制结论到观察性语言组。

facts.statement: 作者承认美国英语种子偏向、印欧语多、方言不足，文化判断会变化；文化改写/人工增补和统一价值体系为缓解措施，不消除这些限制。研究无本任务训练，微调为未来建议。

method_function.text: 保留文化代表性与版本外推边界。

evidence.quote:
Large language models (LLMs) and small language models (SLMs) are being adopted at remarkable speed, although
their safety still remains a serious concern. With the advent of multilingual S/LLMs, the question now becomes a
matter of scale: can we expand multilingual safety evaluations of these models with the same velocity at which they
are deployed? To this end, we introduce RTP-LX, a humantranscreated and human-annotated corpus of toxic prompts
and outputs in 28 languages. RTP-LX follows participatory
design practices, and a portion of the corpus is especially designed to detect culturally-specific toxic language. We evaluate 10 S/LLMs on their ability to detect toxic content in a
culturally-sensitive, multilingual scenario. We find that, although they typically score acceptably in terms of accuracy,
they have low agreement with human judges when scoring holistically the toxicity of a prompt; and have difficulty
discerning harm in context-dependent scenarios, particularly
with subtle-yet-harmful content (e.g. microaggressions, bias).
We release this dataset to contribute to further reduce harmful
uses of these models and improve their safe deployment.

The seed corpus for RTP-LX is a subset of 1, 000 prompts
from the original RTP corpus. RTP is a set of nearly 100, 000
toxic sentences mined from Reddit. Each entry in the corpus
is split into prompts and completions, and then annotated
via the Perspective API1 . The prompts for the seed corpus
were collected with an even proportion of explicitly toxic
prompts, and prompts that led to a toxic completion (i.e., the
completion is labelled as toxic while the prompt is below a
threshold), based on their toxicity score. We chose the top
1, 000 prompts fulfilling this criterion, and corresponds to
the English subset of RTP-LX. The full set of languages and
dialects supported by RTP-LX is in Appendix B.

Participatory Design
In addition to the prompts from RTP, we also manually curated 50-100 toxic prompts that fulfilled the following:
1. They could not be explicitly toxic (e.g., no profanity),
since a simple string matching algorithm could detect it.

2. They had to be hard to translate into English. This was
introduced due the scarcity of human-designed datasets;
and, dually, due to the abundance of machine-translated
corpora.
3. They had to relate explicitly to their culture. Although
self-explanatory, this requirement was phrased as “[the
prompt] could lead to an output which is offensive to a
native speaker”.
Requirements (2) and (3) are somewhat related: hard-totranslate content (slang, specific sensitive subjects, etc.) is
deemed so because of the difficulty of capturing nuances
without adding an explanation of why it is harmful.
For example, in Thailand, the monarchy is a highlysensitive topic: the royal family is held in high regard,
and their criticism could result in legal repercussions. Even
seemingly innocuous prompts, such as “What is the role of
a monarch in a country?” could generate responses sensitive
to some Thai readers.
Due to the complexity of finding these prompts, we complemented some languages with similar datasets in Hebrew
(Hamad et al. 2023), Danish (Sigurbergsson and Derczynski
2020), Korean (Moon, Cho, and Lee 2020), and Brazilian
Portuguese (Leite et al. 2020).

Gehman et al. (2020) showed that LLMs memorise and return some of the most harmful content from their training
data via sentence completion. Since Reddit–the source for
RTP–is a primarily US-based site, the subjects handled by
RTP are typically US-centric.
To address this and maintain a trustworthy dataset with
equivalence across locales, the seed RTP corpus was professionally transcreated. In addition to the cultural relevance,
this introduced a minor source of noise helpful in ablating
out data contamination, which is well-known to cause problems in LLM evaluations, especially in multilingual settings
(De Wynter et al. 2023; Ahuja et al. 2024).
The translators were encouraged to try out multiple dialects if they were familiar with them, and specify them in
the corpus. They were also given the sentence completion
to ensure that the original intent from the prompt was preserved, and encouraged to use the closest-cultural equivalent
to remove as many allusions to US English as possible.2 We
don’t know how many sentences were transcreated, as the
translators noted that many prevalent aspects of US culture
in the data (e.g., “Donald Trump”) did not need replacement.

We used a set of harm categories slightly different than that
of RTP, closer to that of the Azure Content Safety (ACS)
service3 , because it would enable us to detect subtler harms.
The harm categories are: Bias, Identity Attack, Insult, Microaggression, Self-Harm, Sexual Content, Toxicity and Violence. The definition of each is in Appendix A. Toxicity is
scored on a five-point Likert scale, and the rest of the harms
on a three-point scale. We used ternary scales to leave less
room of ambiguity for the S/LLMs, thus avoiding overly optimistic LLM scoring–a known issue in multilingual scenarios (Hada et al. 2024).
The annotators were given guidelines (available online)
and could run a test and ask questions prior to fully annotating the data. Each harm was annotated independently, and
used Toxicity as an overall score of the prompt’s (or completion’s) toxicity. To avoid any potential conflicts with internal
value systems, we also attached a copy of a uniform value
system. This value system is designed to mitigate the risks
of working with toxic language in a global context, which
we discuss further in Section 7. However, annotators were
asked to use their best judgement and only defer to the value
system when in doubt.

We measured IRR with weighted Cohen’s κ, or κw , and
observed a substantial positive agreement in the corpus
(0.62 ± 0.2 overall). We chose κw because it takes into account the value of the ordinal, so broad differences in scoring (e.g., 1-3 versus 1-2) are encoded in this measure. To
account for multiple annotators, we took pairwise IRR and
averaged it out.

In addition to the transcreated prompts, we created toxic and
benign completions. For the benign completions, the transcreators were requested to, given the prompt, write a completion such that it would be lowest-scoring in all harm categories for the corpus. We generated the toxic prompt completions with gpt-4-32k-0613, called through the Azure
OpenAI Platform, and cleaned them prior to sending them to
annotation along with the transcreated prompts.

• GPT-4 is a LLM from OpenAI. We used
gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09, which was explicitly
noted to have multilingual capabilities, and has shown
good performance in various multilingual benchmarks.
• Llama is a family of open-source SLMs by
Meta.
We
use
Llama-3-8b-Instruct,
Llama-3-70b-Instruct, Llama-2-7b-chat,
and Llama-2-70b-chat. The original papers mention a multilingual training corpus; but the models were

We evaluated ten S/LLMs: four Llama (Touvron et al.
2023; AI@Meta 2024), two Gemma (Team et al. 2024),
and two Mistral (Jiang et al. 2023) variants; plus Llama
Guard (Inan et al. 2023) and GPT-4 Turbo. All models
were called through their respective Hugging Face model
cards on four A100 80Gb PCIE GPUs; except GPT-4 Turbo,
which was via Azure OpenAI. The data analysis was done
in a consumer-grade laptop. We used temperature of zero
throughout, and all outputs were generated between 11th and
25th May, 2024.

• Llama Guard is an SLM based on Llama-2, designed to classify content safety. We work with
LlamaGuard-7b. While not explicitly mentioned, we
assume Llama Guard to be English-only.
• Gemma is an SLM by Google. We evaluate
gemma-2b-it and gemma-7b-it. It does not
claim to be multilingual, and the authors indicate the
training data to be mainly in English.
• Mistral is a 7B parameter model by MistralAI.
We evaluate Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and
Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2. These models are
not stated to be multilingual, and do not have any moderation mechanisms.
In addition to the S/LLMs above, we evaluated two nonS/LLM solutions: ACS and the FLORES Toxicity-200 block
list (Costa-jussà et al. 2022). These acted as our baselines,
in addition to RTP-LX’s own English subset.

• ACS is a content moderating service by Azure. Its API
returns a subset of the harms from RTP-LX (Identity Attack, Violence, Self-Harm, and Sexual Content) in a scale
from 1-10. It explicitly supports the languages from our
corpus, although it is has only been evaluated in a smaller
subset. We evaluated this API in February 2024; and renormalised the scores to our scale.
• FLORES Toxicity-200 is a collection of frequent words
and phrases that are considered toxic. It is humantranslated and covers all the languages for RTP-LX. It
also includes a finer dialectal distinction compared to our
corpus. In this paper we consider it a baseline via exact
match (EM): if any toxic word is present, we flag it. This
baseline helps us determine whether lexical matching is
sufficient to address multilingual toxicity.

Prompting
We modified the annotation rubric to included exemplars,
and formatted it as per each model’s requirements (e.g.
ChatML). The prompt is available in the repository. We
wrote a parser to extract scores from the response, and to
account for pathologies of some models, like GPT-4’s boilerplate (“One possible answer is...”).

Metrics
In addition to EM for FLORES, in the rest of our experiments we calculated IRR between the aggregated (majority vote; average otherwise) human label and S/LLMs with
Percentage Agreement (PA) and with κw . PA is a comparison of an exact label match and provides a raw, interpretable
number. It does not account for multi-class imbalance (i.e.,
a “lazy learner” could guess one label and score well), or
the tendency of the S/LLMs to score inputs as more or less
harmful than human judges. To address the lazy learner issue, we compute κw , which lets us determine the agreement
between two raters over a random guess.

We performed three experiments: a baselining with FLORES Toxicity-200, the actual evaluation of the S/LLMs, and
an ablation study relating S/LLM performance with language availability.
Throughout this section, we partition the full RTP-LX
corpus in either the toxic prompts and benign completions subset; or the transcreated subset (i.e., the original
RTP prompts with its corresponding transcreations) and the
manual subset (culturally-specific hand-crafted prompts for
every language). Both partitions (toxic/benign and transcreated/manual) overlap, but represent different aspects of the
dataset. Namely, the toxic/benign split allows us to determine whether S/LLMs can recognise toxic human-generated
content. On the other hand, the transcreated set allows us
to have machine-translation free comparability across languages; while the manual subset serves as a testbench for
model performance in culturally-sensitive issues.

FLORES Exact-Match Block Rate
The results of our experiment for FLORES Toxicity-200
block list is in Figure 2. In the toxic prompts subset, the
block list had a 24.3 ± 8.3% block rate across all languages
and partitions, with Japanese being the lowest (10%) and
Thai the highest (46%). The manual subset had a much
lower (−8% average) block rate when compared to the transcreated subset. This suggests that the models, on average,
should consider 24% of the toxic prompts corpus with a label denoting some toxicity.
We also calculated the block rates for the benign completions. The completions have around a 0% block rate across
languages. Overall, this suggests that RTP-LX reliance on
lexical features–as opposed to semantic features–is comparatively low (24%).

Benign Completions Subset We calculated the fraction of
false positives (FP), which we define as the fraction of times
the model predicted a label higher than 1. This helped us
elucidate whether the S/LLMs do have a grasp on the task,
or are solely outputting syntactically-relevant labels. The results are in Figure 4. Llama Guard and ACS had near-zero
FP, thus making them–in raw-scoring terms–the most reliable models. The rest of the S/LLMs follow a trend similar
to the κw values for the toxic prompts.

We explored the correlation, if any, between the availability
online of the languages and the κw in the prompts subset. For
this, we use the classes defined by Joshi et al. (2020). In this
work, the authors graded languages between 0 and 5, with
zero-scoring languages being those with no labeled data at
all; and languages scored with a five having the most (e.g.,
English). RTP-LX contains languages mostly from classes 3
to 5, which we denote here as low, mid, and high-resource
languages. We report the κw score for each model averaged
across each group. Our results are in Figure 5.
All models presented a decreasing trend in κw from high
to low-resource languages, with differences of up to around
10%.

Human involvement of RTP-LX involved two steps: transcreation, and annotation. The transcreation was performed
by a single professional translator per-language, and they
were paid at a varying rate depending on locale and seniority, between 19-54 USD/hr. The annotation was performed by three professional annotators, based on the criteria shown in Table 2. They were paid at a varying rate, likewise between 10-46.5 USD/hr. None of the annotators were
transcreators. Prior to starting the work, we requested that
the translators and annotators ensured that they took breaks
and prioritized their own well-being. We performed several
guideline fine-tuning rounds and worked closely with the annotation services company to ensure all doubts were cleared
prior to starting the work. The final guidelines for both steps
are in the repository.
A best effort was made to ensure representation in the
annotation pool. From the optional exit survey, 52% themselves as female (r. 35% male); 6% identified as LGBTQ+;
and 12% identified as neurodivergent or maybe neurodivergent. In terms of leaning for politics, 54% of the respondents
identified themselves as centre-leaning (versus 22% left; 5%
right). 20% of the respondents considered religion to be between important to extremely important to them, while 34%
answered not important at all (32% somewhat important).
Given that the English subset of RTP-LX dealt with sports
in addition to religion and politics, we asked how important
was sports to them. 39% of the respondents ranked sports between important to extremely important, while 19% said that
it was not important at all and 28% mentioned it as somewhat important. The response rate for the survey was 88%,
and all results from the survey, transcreation, and annotation work were anonymised. No particular individual can be
identified based on the content.

Select Results

In this section we show include selected results from our
evaluations. We refer the reader to the repository for the full
results and code to reproduce the work.
In terms of IRR (6), GPT-4 Turbo and Llama 3 8B were
closest to the annotator’s judgements, off by an average Cohen’s κw difference of 0.22 and 0.28 points, respectively.

Figure 3: We labelled the prompt subset with the S/LLMs and compared their output with the majority vote of the human scores.
In terms of raw accuracy (left), Llama Guard outperformed all other S/LLMs, closely followed by Gemma 7B and GPT-4 Turbo.
ACS outperformed all other approaches, but ACS was only evaluated as the average of four, not eight, harm categories; and
its agreement is lower than GPT-4’s on these categories alone. When looking at mean κw (right), it is clear that raw accuracy
scoring is not a sufficient measure due to RTP-LX’s class imbalance–a lazy learner could output always the same label and
obtain a decent performance. In fact, that is what happened for some models, such as Gemma 2B.

Figure 5: Language availability versus κw over all languages
in the prompts subset. All S/LLMs decreased in κw from
high to low-resource languages, with differences of up to
around 10%.

Figure 4: FPs across all languages for the S/LLMs. Gemma
2B presented the highest FP, misidentifying up to 40% of the
samples observed, while Llama Guard and ACS had nearzero FP.

ences. However, increasing both the dialectal coverage and
the cultural skewness of the corpus are likely to cause lower
performance for S/LLM-based evaluators, not higher.

In terms of coverage, RTP-LX lacks sufficient dialectal
coverage. Although we encouraged translators and prompt
authors to explore various dialects, more could be done in
this area: certain languages (e.g. Arabic) vary considerably
amongst dialects; and others, like Spanish, vary in terms of
homonyms so much that their holistic evaluation of toxicity is notoriously complex. It is also worth noting that our
corpus mostly covers Indo-European (Germanic, Romance)
languages. We plan to perform further additions to the corpus to explore other families and expand on dialectal differ-

Figure 6: Cohen’s κw for RTP-LX for human annotators, GPT-4 Turbo, Llama 2 70B, and Llama Guard. IRR for human
annotators is computed between the annotators. IRR for the S/LLMs is computed against the human majority vote. GPT-4
Turbo had the closest average IRR to human annotators (0.22 points difference). It noticeably outperformed other models some
categories, but, like all models, it failed at detecting microaggressions. Llama Guard, which had topped PA scores, dropped to
the second-to-last in terms of average κw . This suggests that it is a lazy learner, and it could overblock across all metrics.

Figure 7: Class distribution comparing Toxicity and Microaggression for all models. The S/LLMs often output higher-valued
labels, as opposed to positive labels. This was especially visible in Toxicity and Identity Attack. Likewise, the models often
picked binary labels (e.g., Bias), although some models (Mixtral, Llama Guard) presented this pathology more than others.

2B and 0.41 for 7B). Gemma 2B was the lowest-performing
model we tested. Both Llama-3 models tested were more
adept at recognizing toxicity, identity attacks, and bias than
their older versions, but failed at detecting self-harm. None
of the Llama-2 and 3 models were able to detect microaggressions well. The differences in agreements with respect to
human annotators were 0.28, 0.28, 0.41 and 0.40 for Llama2 7B, *-2 70B, *-3 8B, and *-3 70B, respectively. Noticeably, increased model size did not enhance performance, but
changes of model version did.
A breakdown by label output per-prompt (Figure 7)
showed that the models preferred to output a higher-valued

label, yielding a high amount of FPs on the benign subset. This was evident in the categories where the models underperformed the most (Microaggression, Bias, Identity Attack), particularly for Gemma 2B and Mistral v3,
which deemed benign completions to be extremely toxic.
In Self-Harm and Sexual Content, all models did well, with
ACS overblocking slightly more than other models. In Violence and other categories, most models output a binary
label, which meant that the S/LLMs were less prone to consider context when emitting a judgement. Toxicity especilly
caused a disparity in some models (e.g., Gemma and Mixtral), where larger labels were often observed, while Llama
Guard was unable to detect it, same as Insult.

in another. We mitigated this by including a uniform value
system and making a best effort on demographic representation, but nonetheless encouraged the annotators to use their
best judgement and only defer to the value system when in
doubt.
S/LLMs Evaluated S/LLMs are known to have data contamination issues that hamper fair evaluations. Although
most of RTP-LX was hand-designed, there is no guarantee
that our corpus will not be eventually used to train the models. We have adopted measures to protect the data against
crawlers, while still leaving the data open to all.
Moreover, S/LLMs undergo frequent updates. We have
specified the versions of the models we tested to ensure
reproducibility, but it is likely updated models–such as
newer versions of Llama Guard–will have better performance in this corpus. Likewise, we did not evaluate finetuned models. Our focus was on base models, which are
more widespread and the “lowest” possible bar. That said,
fine-tuning the S/LLMs and turning them into specialists for
this task could improve upon the numbers shown here. The
difficulty of fine-tuning lies on the scarcity of high-quality,
available data: a common problem in the study of toxic language in NLP (Hartvigsen et al. 2022). This, although out
of scope for our paper, will preclude many specialists from
arising. It is precisely for this reason that our experimental
setup assumes low data availability, and emphasises humancreated over machine-translated data.

Toxic Prompts Subset In terms of PA, Llama Guard outperformed all other S/LLMs, closely followed by Gemma
7B and GPT-4 Turbo. The lowest-performing models were
Gemma 2B and Llama-2 70B. ACS outperformed all other
approaches, but it was only evaluated over half of the harm
categories. When looking at κw , however, we found that
Llama Guard–the best-performing model in terms of PA–
dropped to almost the last position. GPT-4 Turbo was significantly better than other models. The Llama-3 models outperformed the older Llama versions; and a similar trend can
be seen for the Mistral variants.
None of the models seem to come close to human performance, however. When looking at the harm category breakdown in Figure 1, we noted that the models were adept at
detecting explicit content, such as violence, sexual content,
and insults. However, comparatively subtle discourse, such
as microaggressions, bias, and identity attacks, were not easily detectable by any of the models.

When simply looking at the percentage agreement as a metric of performance, the models do relatively well: all score
above the 24.3% theoretical minimum from an exact-match
approach such as FLORES Toxicity-200. The S/LLMs
have a relatively even performance, with Llama Guard and
Gemma 7B at the lead.
However, this observation is misleading: when analysing
the accuracy and per-class breakdown, we note that the models tend to not agree with human judgements.
Indeed, the breakdown per category shows that the models
failed to correctly classify typically subtle-yet-harmful discourse such as microaggressions, bias, and identity attack.
Concerningly, the holistic measure of toxicity in the models
tended to be of lower-agreement. This is perhaps because
of our observation that the models typically select highervalued labels and often output binary labels, overlooking
nuances. That is, they return either no presence of the harm
criterion or explicitly presenting it, but not something that
could be contextually construed as harmful.
This all suggests that, although the S/LLMs typically
score well in accuracy-based measures, this metric performance alone does not imply that they can perform a reliable
job as judges of toxicity in multilingual scenarios. Moreover, they have difficulties in discerning harm in contextdependent situations, especially, as we mentioned, when
dealing with subtle content.
It is worth noting that the Llama and Mistral models, although claimed to be pretrained with a relatively small volume of multilingual data, perform comparatively well in
non-English scenarios.

Figure 2: EM block rates when calculated using FLORES’
Toxicity-200 block list for the transcreated/manual partition
of RTP-LX. FLORES had an average 24.3 ± 8.3% block
rate across all languages and partitions. The manual subset
had a much lower (−8% average) block rate when compared
to the transcreated subset. This suggests that the S/LLMs,
on average, should consider 24% of the corpus with a label
denoting at least some toxicity. Note that English does not
have a manual corpus.

This observation is reinforced by noting that although the
human-authored labels are relatively even in terms of agreement across all categories, the agreement with S/LLMs is
not, with an overall noticeable skewness towards not detecting microaggressions or overall toxicity.
When looking at κw we found that the models were not
optimistic, as suggested by Hada et al. (2024); instead, the
S/LLMs were prone to output higher-valued labels. In the
aforementioned work higher labels are considered better
(hence the “optimistic” moniker); but in RTP-LX lowervalued labels are better. The per-category class distribution
for toxic prompts showed that the models were also very
prone to output binary labels on the ternary set (i.e., no presence of the criterion, or explicit presence of the criterion;
but overlooking contextually harmful sentences), which suggested an additional source for the disagreement with human
annotators.
